primitives.name: Burst Parallelism Process
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model Bag-of-tasks benchmark design: launch 5,120 concurrent function invocations of an identical compute payload (Linpack 3408×3408), record per-invocation GFlops and wall-clock behavior, and aggregate mean/SD per memory configuration.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'t': 'time in seconds', 'm': 'memory allocation in MB', 'GFlops': 'giga floating-point operations per second', '\\mathcal{P}(t)': 'parallelism level at time $t$', '\\mu(m)': 'mean GFlops per invocation at memory $m$', '\\sigma^2(m)': 'variance of GFlops at memory $m$'}
primitives.assumptions: Tasks are independent, Linpack GFlops proxies throughput, and concurrency is limited by platform-specific throttles.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When $\mathcal{P}(t) \to 0$, indicating API rate-limiting or resource exhaustion.

layer2.mapping: The burst parallelism process $\mathcal{P}(t)$ mirrors GSE's batch pipeline scheduling, where $\mu(m)$ corresponds to expected throughput and $\sigma^2(m)$ reflects task variability.
layer2.telemetry: Per-invocation GFlops and wall-clock timing data.

primitives.name: Concurrency Ceiling
primitives.verbatim_quote: Hyperparameter analogues: the memory-size sweep is the "tuning" dimension, and the 5,120-task scale is chosen to exceed documented concurrency limits and expose platform throttles.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'C_{\\max}': 'maximum concurrent invocations allowed by platform', 'N_{\\text{tasks}}': 'number of tasks in workload (5120)', 't_{\\text{ramp}}': 'ramp-up time in seconds'}
primitives.assumptions: Platform enforces hard concurrency limits beyond which tasks are queued or rejected.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When $N_{\text{tasks}} > C_{\max}$, leading to throttled or delayed execution.

layer2.mapping: $C_{\max}$ is derived from observed ramp-up curves and API latency outliers, informing GSE's burst pipeline sizing logic.
layer2.telemetry: Time-series of invocation start times and API response latencies.

primitives.name: Billing Granularity Effect
primitives.verbatim_quote: Analysis dimensions: (a) achieved parallelism over time (detecting stepped/rate-limited ramp-up); (b) performance vs allocated memory; (c) API overhead (request latency outliers); (d) billing granularity (100 ms rounding) and its interaction with short tasks.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'T_{\\text{bill}}': 'rounded billing time in milliseconds', 'T_{\\text{exec}}': 'actual execution time in milliseconds', 'C_{\\text{cost}}': 'cost per invocation in USD'}
primitives.assumptions: Cost is rounded to nearest 100 ms, and short tasks are disproportionately affected.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When $T_{\text{exec}} < T_{\text{bill}} < 2T_{\text{exec}}$, cost increases without proportional performance gain.

layer2.mapping: $T_{\text{bill}}$ is computed from $T_{\text{exec}}$ and used to derive marginal cost per task, informing GSE's cost-efficiency thresholds.
layer2.telemetry: Per-invocation execution timestamps and associated billing records.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that burst parallelism $\mathcal{P}(t)$ is a stochastic process defined over memory configurations $m$. Each invocation contributes a random variable $X_i(m)$ with mean $\mu(m)$ and variance $\sigma^2(m)$. The total parallelism at time $t$ is the sum of these variables, approximated by central limit theorem as normal distribution. Concurrency ceiling $C_{\max}$ acts as a hard constraint on the number of simultaneous tasks, causing a step-wise decline in $\mathcal{P}(t)$ when exceeded. Billing granularity introduces a non-linear cost term $C_{\text{cost}}(T_{\text{exec}})$, where $T_{\text{bill}} = \lceil T_{\text{exec}} / 100 \rceil \cdot 100$. These primitives form a dual structure: one for performance (mean/variance) and one for economics (cost-time tradeoff). Failure modes include API throttling, cold starts, and misalignment of network latency with task runtime. The stochastic nature implies that repeated runs may yield different $\mathcal{P}(t)$ curves, necessitating robust statistical inference in GSI.
